## Previously ...

An experiment answers one question well, and you have just computed how long
yours would take. A model asks many questions at once, less well, using data you
already have.

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

- Fit and interpret a linear regression on marketing data
- Read a coefficient as a lever rather than as an algebraic term
- Model diminishing returns, and read an elasticity
- State the conditions under which a coefficient is causal, and notice when they
  fail

# 1. Regression as a Question

## The Question

<!-- Speaker notes: frame the whole lecture as "which levers move the number and
     by how much". No matrix algebra, no derivations, no normal equations. If
     someone wants the maths, point at the reading. -->

> "If I increase spend by €100, what happens to conversions, holding channel and
> week constant?"

. . .

That is the entire lecture. Everything else is the machinery for answering it and
the reasons to distrust the answer.

## Where the Word Comes From

Galton, measuring the heights of parents and children, found that tall parents
have children **closer to average** than themselves.

. . .

He called it "regression to mediocrity". He fitted a straight line to it, and
line-fitting inherited the name.

. . .

So "regression" names a **phenomenon** (Lecture 19's regression to the mean) and
a **method**, and the connection between them is historical rather than logical.
Knowing that saves a lot of confusion.

## Galton's Original Question {.smaller}

![Source: [MGT 100 Customer Analytics, UC San Diego](https://github.com/kennethcwilbur/mgt100) (CC BY 4.0)](./figures/external/mgt100_height_weight_scatter.png){fig-align="center" height="340px"}

*Should you model weight on height, or height on weight? The scatter does not
tell you. The question you are asking does.*


## The Model

```{.python}
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

model = smf.ols("conversions ~ spend + C(channel) + C(week)", data=df).fit()
model.summary()
```

. . .

`C(channel)` and `C(week)` create indicator variables for each category. The
week terms absorb anything that moved every channel at once: a holiday, an
outage, a competitor's campaign.

. . .

**Adding the week terms is the single most important line of this code**, and it
is the one most often left out.

## Reading the Output, In Order of Importance

1. **The coefficient on spend**, in the units of the data. "Each additional €100
   of spend is associated with 1.4 more conversions"
2. **Its confidence interval.** "Between 0.3 and 2.5". This is the finding
3. **The number of observations.** 30 rows and 12 predictors is not a model
4. **R-squared**, last, and mostly ignore it

. . .

R-squared answers "how much of the variation did we describe", which is almost
never the decision. A model with an R-squared of 0.2 and a tight, credible spend
coefficient is more useful than the reverse.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Why does a high R-squared feel like success? Whose question does it answer?
:::

## Holding Constant

"Controlling for channel" means: comparing weeks **within** the same channel,
rather than across channels.

. . .

It does **not** mean the effect of channel has been removed from the world. It
means the comparison no longer confuses "we spent more" with "we spent more on
the expensive channel".

. . .

**You can only control for what you measured.** Everything else is still in
there, quietly, inside the coefficient you are about to quote.

# 2. Extensions Worth Knowing

## Diminishing Returns

The most useful non-linearity in marketing, and the one every media plan
assumes:

. . .

The first €1,000 into a channel reaches the people most likely to respond. The
tenth €1,000 reaches everyone else.

```{.python}
model = smf.ols("conversions ~ np.log1p(spend) + C(channel) + C(week)",
                data=df).fit()
```

. . .

A linear model extrapolated upward says spending €10 million produces 140,000
conversions. **The linear model does not know the market is finite.** The log
model at least bends.

## Elasticity {.smaller}

Take logs of both sides and the coefficient becomes an **elasticity**: the
percentage change in the outcome for a 1% change in the input.

$$\ln q = \alpha + \beta \ln p \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \beta = \frac{d \ln q}{d \ln p}$$

. . .

Scale-free, so it compares across channels, currencies and product lines. This
is why economists reach for it and why it appears in every pricing conversation.

. . .

For price: demand is **elastic** if $\beta < -1$, **inelastic** if
$-1 < \beta < 0$. Revenue is maximised at $\beta = -1$.

. . .

**The constant-elasticity form is popular because it is easy**, and it imposes a
strong assumption: everyone has the same price sensitivity at every price. Often
wrong, occasionally disastrously so.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
If your demand is inelastic, you can raise revenue by raising prices. Why does
that not mean you should?
:::

## Interaction

Does spend work harder on mobile?

```{.python}
model = smf.ols("conversions ~ spend * C(device) + C(week)", data=df).fit()
```

. . .

The interaction term asks whether the **slope** differs by group, not whether the
**level** does. A main effect says mobile converts less; an interaction says
money spent on mobile buys less.

. . .

They are different findings with different budget implications, and they are
routinely confused.

## Logistic Regression

When the outcome is converted / did not convert, at the level of the individual
session:

```{.python}
model = smf.logit("converted ~ C(channel) + C(device) + pages_viewed",
                  data=sessions).fit()
```

. . .

Coefficients are in log-odds, which nobody thinks in. Exponentiate to get an
odds ratio, and say it in words:

> "Sessions from email have about 1.8 times the odds of converting, compared to
> direct, at the same device and page depth."

. . .

**An odds ratio is not a risk ratio.** At low base rates they are close, which is
why the sloppiness usually survives, and at high base rates they are not.

# 3. What Can Go Wrong

## Correlation and Causation, Concretely

Spend rises in December. So do conversions. So does everything.

. . .

Your regression, without week terms, reports that spend causes conversions. It
is describing Christmas.

. . .

**Worse, and more specific to marketing**: budget follows performance. You spend
more on the channel that is working. The regression then reports that spending
causes the performance, when the causation ran the other way through the media
planner.

## Endogeneity, and Why Prices Are the Worst Case

Prices are not set randomly. They rise when demand is strong, or when costs
rise, or when a rival exits.

. . .

Regress quantity on observed price and you measure all of that at once. It is
entirely possible to estimate that **raising prices increases sales**, and to be
correctly reporting what happened.

. . .

**The fix is variation you did not cause and nobody chose**: an experiment
(Lecture 19), a policy change, a cost shock, a competitor's mistake. Without
some source of it, a coefficient is a correlation wearing a lab coat.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Is there anything in your own portfolio data that varied for a reason unrelated
to your marketing? That is your best available natural experiment.
:::

## Endogeneity, With Numbers {.smaller}

![Source: [MGT 100 Customer Analytics, UC San Diego](https://github.com/kennethcwilbur/mgt100) (CC BY 4.0)](./figures/external/mgt100_endogeneity_demand_bias.png){fig-align="center" height="340px"}

*The same data, two specifications. The naive regression says demand is nearly
flat. It is not; the omitted competitor price was doing the work.*


## Omitted Variables

The formal name for the Christmas problem: something you did not include is
driving both the input and the outcome.

. . .

Including a week term fixes seasonality. It fixes nothing about anything else.

. . .

**You cannot test for it.** You can only reason about it, name the candidates
out loud, and say which ones you could not measure. That paragraph in your
report is worth more than another model.

## Multicollinearity

Two channels whose budgets always move together. The model cannot tell them
apart, so it splits the effect between them arbitrarily.

. . .

Symptoms: enormous standard errors, coefficients that flip sign when you add one
variable, a model that predicts well and explains nothing.

. . .

**It is a data problem, not a modelling problem.** No estimator can separate two
things that never moved separately.

## Overfitting

Twelve predictors, thirty rows. The model fits the noise beautifully and
predicts nothing.

. . .

**Marketing datasets are usually small.** Weekly data for two years is 104 rows,
and that is a mature business, not a portfolio site.

. . .

Adding a predictor **always** improves in-sample fit. In-sample fit is therefore
not evidence of anything, and R-squared going up is not news.

## Four Fits to the Same Points {.smaller}

![Source: [MGT 100 Customer Analytics, UC San Diego](https://github.com/kennethcwilbur/mgt100) (CC BY 4.0)](./figures/external/mgt100_overfitting.png){fig-align="center" height="340px"}

*R-squared rises all the way across. Only one of these would survive contact
with new data.*


## Retrodiction and Cross-Validation {.smaller}

**Retrodiction**: retrospective prediction. Hide some data, fit on the rest,
predict the hidden part, measure the error.

The algorithm:

1. Split the data into $K$ folds at random
2. Hold out fold $k$, fit on the other $K-1$, predict fold $k$, store the errors
3. Repeat for every $k$, then for every candidate model
4. Keep the model with the lowest average prediction error

. . .

**Two honest caveats.** Cross-validation is one input to model choice, not the
criterion, and it matters most when prediction is the actual goal. And on
marketing time series, random folds leak the future into the past: split by time
instead.

## How Cross-Validation Works {.smaller}

![Source: [DS701 Tools for Data Science, Boston University](https://github.com/tools4ds/DS701-Course-Notes)](./figures/external/ds701_k_fold_cv.png){fig-align="center" height="310px"}

*Hold out a fold, fit on the rest, score on the fold, rotate. Average the
scores. This is the whole idea.*


## Simpler Than You Think

**Simple models perform similarly to complicated ones on small and medium
data.** With enough data most flexible models converge to similar performance
anyway.

. . .

Regularisation methods (lasso, ridge) penalise complexity on the theory that
simpler models predict better out of sample. Worth knowing the names, and worth
knowing they are a response to this same problem.

. . .

On 100 rows of marketing data, the argument for a neural network is almost never
statistical.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
If a simple model performs as well, what is the argument for the complicated
one? Are there good ones?
:::

## The Trade-Off You Are Actually Making {.smaller}

![Source: [MGT 100 Customer Analytics, UC San Diego](https://github.com/kennethcwilbur/mgt100) (CC BY 4.0)](./figures/external/mgt100_bias_variance.png){fig-align="center" height="310px"}

*Too simple and you underfit; too flexible and you fit the noise. The
minimum of the error curve is not at either end.*


## When to Trust a Coefficient

A checklist, in order:

1. Is the sign what theory would predict? If not, stop and find out why
2. Is the interval narrow enough that both ends imply the same decision?
3. Did you control for time, and did the coefficient survive it?
4. Can you name the omitted variable that worries you most, and rule it out?
5. Would the coefficient change a decision, at either end of its interval?
6. **Or could you run the experiment from Lecture 19 instead?**

. . .

If you reach 6 and the answer is yes, the model was a way of avoiding the
experiment.

## The Misuse Question

A model that predicts well can still be one you should not deploy.

. . .

Before acting on a customer-level model, ask: is it **effective, legal, moral,
private, conspicuous**, and how will customers react if they notice?

. . .

The guiding principle, not a rule: **using data to genuinely serve a customer's
interest is usually fine. Using private data against their interest can harm
people, break laws and end a business.** GDPR is the version of this you are
subject to, and Lecture 4 covered it.

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

Using your joined traffic and spend data:

1. Fit a regression of conversions on spend with channel and week controls
2. Report the spend coefficient with its confidence interval, in plain English
3. Refit with `log1p(spend)` and say which fits your beliefs about the world
   better, and why
4. Name one omitted variable that could be driving the result
5. State what experiment would settle the question, and what it would cost in
   weeks

**30 minutes**

# 4. AI for Model Criticism

## AI This Block: An analyst you interrogate

Where we are on the module's AI spine, introduced in Lecture 10:

> **An analyst you interrogate**

## Omitted Variables Are a Listing Problem

Naming candidate confounders is exactly what a broadly-read assistant is good
at, because it is recall over a large literature rather than judgement about your
business.

> "I regressed conversions on spend with channel and week controls, and got a
> positive spend coefficient. List every variable that could be driving this
> that I have not included. Order them by how likely they are to matter for a
> small service business in Ireland."

. . .

Then the follow-up that does the work: **"which of those could I actually
measure, and which would I have to argue about instead?"**

## Reading the Output Together

Pasting a `model.summary()` and asking for a plain-English reading is reliable,
fast, and a good way to catch a misread coefficient.

. . .

Asking whether the result is **causal** is not. It cannot see your data
generating process, it will accept your framing, and it will produce a
well-structured paragraph either way.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
It will tell you that correlation is not causation, and then interpret your
coefficient causally three sentences later. Why is that failure so hard to
notice?
:::

## What It Cannot Do

- Know which of the confounders it listed is actually present in your business
- Tell you whether your data can settle the question, unless you make it compute
  something
- Notice that your 30 rows cannot support 12 predictors, unless you ask
- Choose the functional form on grounds other than fit

. . .

**You supply the context, it supplies the checklist.** Block 4's rule,
unchanged.

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

1. Fit your regression and paste the summary
2. Ask for a plain-English reading of the spend coefficient, with its interval
3. Ask for candidate omitted variables, ordered by plausibility
4. Say which one you could actually measure
5. Ask it to argue that your coefficient is **not** causal, and see whether its
   argument is better than yours

**15 minutes**
